ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: (2016 · Shandong Weifang No. 1 Middle School monthly exam) In the electric field shown in the figure, the equipotential surfaces are a cluster of mutually parallel vertical planes, with intervals all d, and the potentials of the surfaces have been marked in the figure. Now a charged small ball of mass m (which can be regarded as a point charge) enters the electric field obliquely upward with speed v0, in a direction making a 45° angle with the horizontal direction. To make the small ball move in a straight line, the electric property and amount of charge carried by the small ball are (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In the electric field shown in the figure, the equipotential surfaces are a cluster of mutually parallel vertical planes, with intervals all d, and the potentials of the surfaces have been marked in the figure. Now a charged small ball of mass m (which can be regarded as a point charge) enters the electric field obliquely upward with speed v0, in a direction making a 45° angle with the horizontal direction. If the small ball is to move in a straight line, what electric property should the small ball carry? What is the amount of charge?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, a set of mutually parallel vertical dashed lines can be seen, representing vertical equipotential surfaces; the potentials marked from left to right are respectively -200 V, -100 V, 0, 100 V, 200 V, and adjacent equipotential surfaces are equally spaced. The initial velocity arrow v0 of the charged small ball points to the upper right, and the angle with the horizontal dashed line is marked as 45°. Reasoning: The potential difference between adjacent equipotential surfaces is 100 V, and the interval is d, so the magnitude of the uniform electric field is E=Δφ/d=100/d. The electric field direction points from high potential to low potential; since the potential in the figure increases to the right, the electric field direction is horizontally to the left. The small ball is subjected to gravity mg vertically downward and the electric field force. To make the small ball move in a straight line under a constant resultant force, the resultant force must be collinear with the initial velocity direction. The initial velocity is along the upper right 45°, and gravity is downward, so the electric field force should be horizontally to the left, and its magnitude should be equal to mg, so that the resultant force is lower left 45°, collinear and opposite to the initial velocity. Since the electric field direction is to the left, and the electric field force also needs to be to the left, the small ball carries positive charge. From qE=mg, q·(100/d)=mg is obtained, and solving gives q=mgd/100.
